Context-Free Rewriting (CFR) is a rewriting framework that extends Context-Free Grammars by allowing the right-hand side of a production rule to be a nonterminal symbol paired with a regular expression. This paper introduces Context-Header Rewrite (CHR), a novel rewriting formalism that generalizes CHR by permitting rule right-hand sides to be defined as a sequence of CFR production rules. We demonstrate that, despite this increased expressivity, every language recognized by CHR can be characterized by a specific type of CFR grammar. This finding establishes that CHR retains the same expressive power as conventional CFGs, a property we term "articulate power." Our proof relies on a canonical form for CHR productions, which we also show to be of practical value. Specifically, we apply this canonical form to show that any CHR grammar capable of generating an infinite string set can be transformed into a linear-time equivalent that is also in such canonical form.

We investigate the potential for a global asymmetry in the sense of rotation among galaxies, a phenomenon predicted by some cosmological models. By analyzing the Dark Energy Survey (DES), we identified 1,000 galaxies with measured rotation directions, enabling a statistical test of this asymmetry. Our results indicate no significant asymmetry, with a p-value of 0.44. We further demonstrate that a mild preference for counter-clockwise rotation persists even when examining only galaxies with redshifts below 0.1. To assess the robustness of this finding, we compared our DES data with similar catalogs from four other surveys: the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), the Two Micron All Sky Survey (2MASS), the Two Degree Field (2DF), and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Early Data Release (SDSS EDR). All five datasets yield consistent null results, with p-values ranging from 0.11 to 0.71. These findings support the conclusion that a global asymmetry in galaxy rotation is not supported by observational evidence.

Meta-learning seeks to derive a generalized prior from a collection of source tasks, facilitating rapid adaptation to novel challenges. While practical applications often involve noisy data, existing research predominantly addresses clean source tasks, neglecting the impact of label corruption on meta-optimization. This study investigates how label noise within source tasks influences meta-learning performance. We demonstrate that the conventional empirical risk minimization approach, which aggregates gradients across tasks, is highly susceptible to noise from individual sources. To mitigate this, we introduce a sampling technique that randomly aggregates multiple tasks per iteration, thereby reducing the impact of corrupted data. We further prove that the optimal learning direction in a two-task scenario can be characterized by a low-rank matrix decomposition. Leveraging this insight, we propose Eigen-Reptile, a novel algorithm that identifies a direction via such decomposition and updates the model using only noise-free tasks. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets with label noise confirm that Eigen-Reptile surpasses current state-of-the-art methods.

We introduce ICAM-reg, a framework designed to derive interpretable insights from individual scans of brain structure and function. This approach utilizes a single-instance learning method that integrates the strengths of both deep learning and traditional machine learning. The system employs a deep neural network to extract high-level features, which are then fed into a random forest regressor to predict continuous variables. To ensure the reliability of these predictions, we implement a feature attribution technique that quantifies how each high-level feature contributes to the final output. This strategy offers a transparent and robust method for understanding the relationship between complex, high-level patterns and specific clinical or behavioral traits in individual subjects. We applied this framework to the UK Biobank dataset to investigate the link between brain connectivity and cognitive performance. The results demonstrate that the model can accurately forecast cognitive scores and identify the specific brain regions and connections that drive these predictions.

This paper investigates ethical frameworks in AI by focusing on the underexamined spaces between explicit moral rules: the margins. These include areas such as the misalignment between intended rules and unintended actions, as well as the gaps between existing rules and emerging situations. By analyzing these marginal cases, we demonstrate how they can generate novel ethical dilemmas, as well as how they might be leveraged to enhance the robustness of AI systems.

The paper examines the collection of finite languages over a fixed alphabet that contain an integer number of elements not exceeding $n$. We label these collections as the " extents" corresponding to $n$. For any regular language, it is a known fact that there exists a unique associated sequence of extents indexed by $n$. We establish that the collection of all such sequences precisely matches the collection of $\omega$-regular languages.

This study introduces a deep learning-based approach for wireless channel assessment and forecasting within cell-free massive MIMO (CFmMIMO) systems, accounting for channel degradation. The method utilizes the alternating projection (ALP) technique to evaluate the channel state, effectively mitigating the computational burden associated with the high dimensionality of CFmMIMO channel matrices. Subsequently, a recurrent neural network (RNN) forecasts future channel states, utilizing both the current state and historical data from the preceding time slot. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed ALP-based assessment method achieves performance comparable to that of a full channel state information (CSI) benchmark. Furthermore, the RNN-based forecasting model significantly outperforms a traditional linear auto-regressive model in terms of accuracy.

This study examines the impact of including lattice QCD results on $|{\cal M}_{11}|$ within the calculation of radiative corrections to the $p$-process, specifically analyzing its effect on the $|{\cal M}_{11}|$ value. We find that incorporating these results significantly alters the value of $|{\cal M}_{11}|$, with the magnitude of this change varying depending on the specific lattice calculation employed.

This paper introduces Identity Augmented Residual Image Denoising (IRID), a novel deep neural network designed for image denoising. The architecture comprises a residual branch and a skip connection branch, with the former utilizing a noise-aware U-Net structure and the latter relying on a noise-agnostic convolutional block. The key innovation lies in the noise-aware residual branch, which employs a residual-in-residual design and incorporates a dedicated identity stream. This stream, derived from the original clean image, provides the model with the necessary identity information to facilitate effective feature extraction. The proposed identity stream is trained alongside the residual components, and its necessity is validated through ablation studies. Empirical results demonstrate that IRID outperforms current state-of-the-art denoising techniques across various datasets, particularly in handling high-variance noise.

Correlation-driven approaches, including self-supervised learning and self-supervised guidance, have proven highly effective in computer vision. However, their limitations regarding sample efficiency and robustness to spurious correlations remain unresolved. This study introduces a theoretical framework for analyzing these methods through the lens of latent correlation-driven multi-view learning. We demonstrate that these methods can be conceptualized as multi-view learning where views are generated by the latent state conditioned on task-specific variables, thereby inheriting their strengths and weaknesses. Specifically, we prove that recovering the true state is feasible when the number of views is sufficiently large, provided the signal-to-noise ratio is high. Furthermore, we establish that self-guidance degrades performance when the auxiliary task relies on noisy labels, and we further show that the method fails to learn the true state if the auxiliary task is corrupted by adversarial perturbations. Empirical evaluations on image classification and object detection confirm the practical validity of our theoretical findings.

We investigate the mid-infrared (MIR) characteristics of galaxies exhibiting exceptionally high MIR colours, defined as $S_{12\mu m}-S_{3.6\mu m} > 2.5$ mag, utilizing data from the Spitzer Space Telescope's IRAC and MIPS instruments. Our analysis reveals that these galaxies are typically located at redshifts $z < 0.5$, possess high star formation rates, and reside in dense environments. While their MIR emission is dominated by star formation, it is significantly amplified by dust heated by shocks from supernovae and galactic winds. These properties suggest that the sample consists of star-forming systems with intense, rapid outflows. We examine the MIR colours of these galaxies in the context of the MIR-UV relation, noting that they align with the star-forming branch of the relation. However, they exhibit a distinct trend: as the UV slope steepens, the MIR slope flattens, indicating that the MIR flux is increasingly driven by shock heating. We also explore the potential for these galaxies to be misclassified as AGN due to their intense MIR emission. Our findings indicate that while MIR colours alone are insufficient to identify AGN, they can serve as a diagnostic tool to distinguish between star-forming and AGN-dominated systems.

We investigate how moral principles are applied by language models when making decisions, drawing inspiration from the "exception handling" framework prevalent in human psychology. This framework posits that humans rely on a default rule in most scenarios but switch to specific exceptions when unique contextual factors arise. We introduce a novel task designed to assess a model's ability to generate moral decisions, specifically focusing on its capacity to identify appropriate conditions for creating exceptions. Our findings reveal that, contrary to the common belief that humans frequently deviate from defaults, individuals actually create exceptions very rarely. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that language models are adept at replicating the conditions under which humans typically depart from their standard rules.

This work investigates the properties of valuation domains by examining the limits of sequences of non-noetherian complete intersection rings. We introduce a specific class of valuation domains termed "of complete intersection type" and demonstrate that their singular locus corresponds precisely to the limit, under the flat topology, of the singular loci found within the sequence of these complete intersection rings.

This study addresses the challenges of numerically solving the Dirac equation in two dimensions, specifically for a particle interacting with an external potential. We begin by examining the consequences of the non-local nature inherent in Dirac operators, which poses significant difficulties for standard numerical methods. To overcome these issues, we introduce a technique to transform the non-local Dirac equation into a local one, accompanied by a new discretization approach. This method successfully captures the physical characteristics of Dirac fermions, notably the Klein paradox, while also enabling the computation of the equation's Green's function.

This paper investigates how intermittent communication disruptions influence collaborative adaptive cruise control (CACC) and vehicle platoons within a traffic environment. The study employs a realistic platoon model that accounts for longitudinal dynamics, including the effects of wind disturbances and varying road grades. The analysis utilizes a nonlinear, disturbance-observer-based adaptive control framework to estimate and mitigate these disturbances. The core CACC controller is designed using linear quadratic regulator (LIR) theory, with longitudinal inter-vehicle distance serving as the primary safety constraint. The research evaluates both linear and nonlinear road profiles, demonstrating that the proposed adaptive controller effectively mitigates wind and gradient disturbances. Furthermore, it is shown that maintaining platooning stability is feasible even amidst communication disruptions, provided that specific safety distances are observed.

In recent years, the reliability of information on social media has become increasingly critical. While Twitter serves as a valuable platform for news and information sharing, it is often plagued by unreliable content. This study introduces a novel approach to evaluating Twitter users' credibility. The method integrates a user's activity level with their receiving score, which measures the volume of positive or negative reactions (likes, retweets, favorites) they garner. By analyzing these interactions, the system can assess whether a user is likely to disseminate false information. We evaluated this approach using a dataset of 10,000 users, comparing our generated reliability scores against existing received scores and user following counts. The results indicate that our proposed metric outperforms traditional received scores in accurately predicting user trustworthiness.

This paper introduces a new framework for on-demand learning in Vehicular Ad-hoc Networks (V2X), designed to adapt to the dynamic nature of vehicular environments. The system employs a learning mechanism that evolves alongside the environment, enabling it to learn the characteristics of urgent traffic slices in real time. The framework's efficacy is demonstrated through a specific use case: a roadside unit (RSU) that must dynamically allocate radio resources to a vehicle experiencing an emergency, such as a sudden brake, without prior knowledge of the required slice parameters. The study evaluates the framework's performance across various scenarios, highlighting its ability to learn and adapt effectively. The results indicate that this approach achieves rapid convergence, allowing the system to learn the necessary slice details within a few seconds.

The rapid advancement of robotics and artificial intelligence is driving the development of automated systems and collaborative robots (cobots) designed to work alongside humans. However, these technologies introduce new challenges, including the need for enhanced safety measures and improved human-robot interaction. This paper introduces CoHaptics, a novel human-robot cooperative system that utilizes haptic feedback to improve safety and efficiency within a factory environment. The CoHaptics framework comprises three primary elements: a robotic arm, a human operator, and a haptic device. The system operates by having the robotic arm execute a predefined task while the human operator performs a secondary task. When the human's movement creates a potential collision risk with the robot, a warning signal is generated and transmitted to the haptic device, which delivers tactile feedback to the operator. This feedback prompts the human to adjust their trajectory, thereby preventing accidents. Experimental results indicate that CoHaptics significantly boosts safety and operational efficiency in factory settings. Furthermore, this study offers valuable insights for the design of future collaborative systems that integrate tactile feedback mechanisms.

This study introduces a new framework for analyzing city-wide Socio-Tech systems, offering a distinct perspective compared to conventional analyses. Rather than treating socio-technology as a singular, monolithic entity, we reconceptualize it as a collection of autonomous agents: citizens, technologies, and movements. Consequently, our framework models the urban landscape as a complex ecosystem of interactions among these three components. By examining the interplay between citizens and technologies, we identify the emergence of movements, which subsequently drive the evolution of both tech and civic life. This approach enables a deeper understanding of the dynamics within city-wide Socio-Tech systems, particularly regarding the lifecycle of movements, their impact on technological advancement, and the mechanisms of their formation.

This paper investigates online caching within a framework where the system possesses knowledge of request arrival times, although the specific identities of the requests remain unknown. This scenario is modeled as an online set cover problem, where the objective is to minimize the number of cache accesses by selecting a minimal cover of the required item sets. We introduce a novel algorithm that achieves near-optimality by leveraging knowledge of the optimal solution for the problem restricted to a smaller subset of requests. Specifically, the algorithm identifies the optimal cover for a designated set of requests $R$ and subsequently determines a minimal cover for the remaining requests $R \setminus R$. The performance of the algorithm is analyzed under the assumption that the optimal cover for the smaller set is a subset of the cover for the entire request set. We establish that the algorithm's competitive ratio is bounded by $\frac{n}{k} + \frac{1}{\alpha}$, where $n$ denotes the number of cache items, $k$ represents the cache size, and $\alpha$ corresponds to the optimality of the cover for the smaller request set. This finding is significant because it demonstrates that competitive ratios can be significantly improved when the optimal cover for a smaller set of requests is known.

Accurate and timely image segmentation is vital for clinical decision-making, particularly in emergency and critical care scenarios. While deep learning has become a leading approach for medical image segmentation, most existing methods are computationally intensive, making them unsuitable for real-time applications. To address this, we introduce the Trilateral Focus Network (TFN), a novel architecture designed for efficient real-time segmentation. TFN integrates three key components: a multi-scale feature extraction module, a spatial feature enhancement module, and a class-aware feature refinement module. Experimental results on the Kvasir-SEG and CT-SEG benchmarks demonstrate that TFN achieves a mean Dice score of 0.919 and 0.889, respectively, while maintaining a processing speed of 25.6 frames per second.

This study introduces the linearized, off-shell framework for the geometry of 11-dimensional supergravity, built from a linearized version of the 4+7 supergeometry that characterizes full 11-d supersymmetry. This linearized 4+7 supergeometry is defined through a 4-dimensional Lorentzian superworldvolume, a 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic 4+7 superworldvolume, a hyperbolic

Data quality is a critical factor in data science, as the quality of input data directly influences the quality of model outputs. This paper introduces a novel approach to enhance data quality by leveraging the training dynamics of Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDMs). The method involves training a GBDM sequentially on subsets of data that exhibit increasing levels of quality. We demonstrate that this strategy not only yields superior model performance but also provides a practical metric for assessing data quality.

We examine the unitary mapping between qubits and the anyonic degrees of freedom inherent in the quantum Hall effect. This mapping reveals that the anyonic qubit possesses distinct properties compared to the standard fermionic or bosonic qubit. Specifically, we demonstrate that any local unitary operation on the anyonic qubit inevitably alters its topological order. Furthermore, we argue that any operation preserving the topological structure of the anyonic qubit must be globally defined rather than strictly local.

We introduce a novel approach to address the noise inherent in the objective functions of denoising pretraining for large-scale Autoencoder Language Models (ALMs). This approach leverages the model's own predictions to identify and mitigate contamination within the training data. We evaluate our method on two objectives: (1) enhancing the quality of the final fine-tuning performance and (2) reducing the computational cost of pretraining by filtering out noisy instances early. Our results indicate that our method improves performance across both tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the approach is highly efficient, requiring only 1.5% additional computational overhead during pretraining while yielding a 10% improvement in performance on downstream tasks.

Quantum networks are essential for the future of quantum information processing, yet constructing them is a complex task that requires precise knowledge of their topology. This knowledge is vital for designing efficient routing protocols and optimizing the performance of distributed quantum applications. This work introduces a methodology to infer the topology of quantum networks using only local measurements at individual nodes. We demonstrate that the connectivity of a quantum network can be identified by analyzing the statistical properties of its local Bell parameters. This approach is validated through numerical simulations, which reveal that the topology can be accurately recovered even from noisy data. These findings suggest that inferring quantum network topology via local measurements is feasible and could serve as a practical tool for engineering and managing these networks.

Information Vizing (IV) plays a vital role in conveying data insights, yet many individuals struggle to comprehend the variety of IV types available. While a common solution involves providing written descriptions, these often fail to engage readers effectively. This study introduces crowdsourced sample-based IV descriptions as an alternative method to elucidate IV concepts. We conducted a crowdsourcing study gathering 1,000 IV descriptions, each containing five samples, to analyze how these samples influence comprehension. Our findings indicate that sample-based descriptions significantly enhance understanding, particularly for viewers with lower reading levels. Furthermore, the study highlights that the selection of samples is critical; specific IV types require different illustrative examples to be clear.

This study demonstrates that the ground state of a system with $N$ electrons in a $d$-dimensional box, subject to a uniform external potential, is always a peak entropy condensate (PEC). This conclusion relies on a proof of an $L^1$ bound for the Fourier transform of the one-particle density matrix, which establishes the convergence of the associated Fourier series. This finding validates an earlier hypothesis made by the same author and confirms a conjecture raised by Lieb in 1968.

Counterfactual reasoning is a critical component of decision-making, enabling agents to refine their policies by analyzing discrepancies between anticipated and actual outcomes. However, this approach is frequently compromised by model bias, which arises when the estimated outcome distribution diverges from the true distribution. This paper investigates how such distributional uncertainty influences the efficacy of counterfactual learning. We demonstrate that counterfactual methods can outperform standard approaches in specific contexts, yet we also reveal that they are susceptible to model bias, which may result in suboptimal decisions. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel algorithm designed to mitigate the effects of distributional uncertainty. We establish that this method is robust against model bias and maintains strong performance across various environments. Empirical evaluations across multiple settings confirm that this new algorithm achieves superior performance compared to existing baselines.

Urban noise categorization is essential for assessing and mitigating noise pollution. This paper presents a categorization framework that leverages both spectro-temporal and statistical features to identify noise types. We introduce a new dataset comprising 100 hours of recordings from 10 distinct noise categories, collected across 10 different cities. This dataset is intended to facilitate cross-location and cross-urban categorization research. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed features effectively support urban noise classification.

We examine the properties of supersymmetric AdS$_4$ black holes within the framework of $N=3$ and $N=4$ gauged supergravity models coupled to vector multiplets representing substance fields. The electrically charged counterparts are linked to solutions featuring dyonic configurations and those possessing vanishing electric charge. Specifically, we investigate the existence of supersymmetric solutions for this class of models, deriving explicit expressions for the corresponding black hole metrics and gauge potentials. Furthermore, we calculate the associated entropy and demonstrate that it aligns perfectly with the entropy formula derived from the asymptotic boundary conditions.

Focal-Plane Processor-Array Sensor-Processors (FP3s) are emerging as a promising technology for edge computing in machine vision, offering a distinct advantage by integrating sensing and processing directly on-chip. This integration enables rapid, low-power, and energy-efficient inference for machine learning tasks. However, a significant hurdle remains: the lack of software tools capable of automatically converting convolutional neural network (CNN) operations into efficient kernels for these architectures. This paper introduces Cain, a new framework designed to automate the creation of FP-SP optimized kernels. Cain operates in two stages: first, it automatically synthesizes C++ code for specific convolutional kernels, and second, it compiles this code into machine code tailored for the target processor. To ensure efficiency, Cain employs a hybrid approach combining both dataflow and instruction-level parallelism. Experimental results demonstrate that Cain-generated code achieves a speedup of 1.5x to 10.5x over existing state-of-the-art kernels on FP-SPs.

We examine the low-energy effective field theory of Type IIB string theory, incorporating both non-Abelian and U(1) factors within its gauge symmetry. We establish that any U(1) gauge symmetry surviving from an $\mathcal{N}=1$ supergravity theory derived via F-theory compactification on an elliptically fibered Calabi-Yau threefold must be free of mixed anomalies with respect to the identity element, thereby permitting a global symmetry-breaking mechanism. This finding aligns with the established conjecture that such a U(1) must couple to a discrete theta term. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this theta term can be extended to a continuous range, contingent upon the inclusion of a specific class of axion-like fields.

This work examines Nash equilibrium learning in a game-theoretic framework where agents possess a shared virtual environment and interact through a reward function defined by the environment. While the game-theoretic approach facilitates the learning of equilibria, it faces challenges due to the vast state-action space inherent in such simulations. To address this, we introduce a novel pruning mechanism that reduces the effective size of the state-action space by eliminating transitions that cannot be part of an equilibrium. We demonstrate that this pruning method is both sound and complete, and empirical results indicate that it significantly accelerates convergence toward an equilibrium.
We introduce a natural deduction framework for Aristotle's modal syllogism, which is subsequently applied to derive the modal versions of the first figure's rules for Aristotle's logic.

This study examines the quantum causal structure of a bipartite system, specifically focusing on detection vulnerabilities. We demonstrate that a quantum causal structure is uniquely determined by the set of states that are causally detectable. Furthermore, we establish that the ability to detect causation within composite quantum systems is driven by specific correlations among subsystems. Our findings indicate that while entanglement is a prerequisite for detecting causation in composite quantum systems, it alone is insufficient. We also prove that detection vulnerability arises from the inherent ability to choose a subsystem basis for measurement. Finally, we show that both the ability to detect causation and the susceptibility to detection vulnerability can be quantified using quantum correlation measures.

This study introduces a dual-critic reinforcement learning (RL) framework designed to optimize frame-level bit allocation for HEVC/H.265 video streams. The proposed architecture integrates a "prediction" critic to anticipate the optimal bit allocation for the current frame and a "propagation" critic to forecast residual coding efficiency for subsequent frames. This dual-critic approach effectively captures the inter-frame dependencies inherent in video compression. Experimental results indicate that the method achieves an average gain of approximately 1.5% in Bjøntegaard distortion (BD-rate) relative to the standard rate-distortion optimization method operating at the frame level.

We investigate the chemical evolution of proto-planetary disks, specifically focusing on the transition from carbon-rich to oxygen-rich environments. Our findings indicate that the destruction of resistant carbon grains in the outer disk regions triggers a chemical shift toward an oxygen-dominated composition. This process is driven by the thermal decomposition of refractory polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and graphite, which releases substantial amounts of carbon into the gas phase. This release lowers the abundance of gaseous carbon relative to oxygen, thereby facilitating the transition to oxygen-rich chemistry. This mechanism is particularly significant in disks with high accretion rates, where the central heating of the midplane elevates temperatures sufficiently to destroy these refractory grains. Consequently, the depletion of carbon-rich grains in the outer disk acts as a catalyst for the chemical transition from carbon-rich to oxygen-rich conditions.

Cutting plane methods are widely used to address various mixed-integer programming (MIP) challenges. Central to these approaches is the selection of cutting planes, a task traditionally managed by human experts. This paper introduces a machine learning framework designed to automate this selection process. We define a Markov Decision Process (MDP) where the objective is to maximize the count of feasible cutting planes added to the MIP relaxation. We develop a forward-looking policy network capable of selecting cutting planes by leveraging this MDP structure. Additionally, we present a novel data generation strategy that enables policy networks trained on synthetic data to generalize effectively to instances unseen during training. Empirical results indicate that our method outperforms existing heuristic and machine learning-based selection tools.

We report on the superconducting properties of $\mathrm{Mo}_{0.9}\mathrm{Ir}_{0.1}\mathrm{Te}_{2}$, a doped Weyl semimetal featuring broken inversion symmetry. Despite this symmetry breaking, the material maintains a low effective mass for carriers, resulting in a high $T_{\mathrm{C}}$ of $10.5\,\mathrm{K}$ and a high upper critical field $H_{\mathrm{C2}}$ of $22.5\,\mathrm{T}$. These findings are consistent with a strong-coupling superconducting state, evidenced by a BCS $H_{\mathrm{c2}}(0)$ ratio of $2.14$ and a normalized $H_{\mathrm{c2}}(0)/T_{\mathrm{C}}$ value of $0.176\,\mathrm{T/K}$. Furthermore, the material exhibits a high Ginzburg-Landau parameter $\kappa$ of $0.36$, indicating type-II superconductivity.

Software development relies on bug reporting tools to report software defects, a process that often consumes significant time and resources. To address this, we introduce an automated system that leverages pre-trained language models to classify bug reports into specific categories, including performance, security, functional, and other issues. By employing a hybrid architecture that integrates BERT with a custom classifier, we achieved an F1 score of 0.89 on the testing dataset.

We investigate the electronic properties of nonisotropic graphene, specifically analyzing the impact of uniaxial strain on its anisotropy. This analysis reveals that the strain-induced anisotropy can induce a transition between various electronic phases, including a semimetal, a metal, and an insulator. We demonstrate that within the framework of the $t$-$J$ model, this system undergoes a transition from a semimetal to a metal, followed by a subsequent shift from a metal to an insulator. Furthermore, we examine the characteristics of these transitions and determine the critical values of the $t$ and $J$ parameters associated with them.

This study introduces a new approach to remotely supervised named entity identification (RE NIE) that addresses the challenge of identifying entity types in unseen categories. By leveraging a teacher-student framework, the system first employs an instructor model to generate predictions for unseen types, which are then used as pseudo-labels to train a student model. To enhance the student model's performance, we developed an adaptive instructor learning strategy that dynamically adjusts prediction probabilities based on the student's current capabilities. Additionally, we implemented a fine-grained student ensemble method to further boost accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Social media has become a primary source for gathering user-generated content regarding travel experiences. This study presents a case analysis of a Twitter dataset to extract such data, specifically focusing on identifying key locations and categorizing sentiments. Furthermore, the paper introduces a novel method for classifying travel experiences into distinct types, including holidays, business trips, and exploring local culture.

The Information-Focused Characteristic Relations (IFCR) framework is a novel method for learning microstructure characteristics from macroscopic responses. This approach constructs a data-driven mapping between these domains by identifying a latent space that represents the true microstructural features. The resulting mapping is utilized to predict macroscopic behavior given specific microstructural configurations. To achieve this, the study employs a two-stage process: first, an autoencoder learns an encoder-decoder transformation to map microstructure data into a latent space, while simultaneously optimizing the latent space's dimensionality; second, a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) is trained to map these latent representations to macroscopic responses. The effectiveness of this strategy is validated through two case studies: predicting the effective elastic properties of 2D random fiber-reinforced composites and the effective plastic response of 2D polycrystalline aggregates.

We report the discovery of a 2 Myr-old planetary companion orbiting the Herbig Ae star CI Tau, detected via high-contrast direct imaging. Utilizing the Gemini Planet Imager (GPI) and the Coronagraphic Imager with Adaptive optics (CIAO) on the Gemini North 10m telescope, we identified the planet at a separation of 11.5 arcseconds (approximately 100 au) in the near-infrared. The object exhibits a brightness of $m_{\rm K_s} = 12.6 \pm 0.1$ mag and $m_{\rm H} = 12.9 \pm 0.1$ mag, with a 3$\sigma$ contrast limit of 2.5 mag at 100 au. The observed flux is consistent with a 1 Myr-old planetary model possessing a radius of 1.5 Jupiter masses and a temperature of 1000 K. This study introduces a fresh potential for studying off-center circular orbits. By employing the superposition of a Coulomb and a quadratic potential, we identify a specific parameter range where these orbits exist. Additionally, we provide analytical proofs for both the constancy of the orbit radius and the stability of circular paths within the defined parameter set.

This paper examines the connection between the existence of a global best Sobolev inequality and the presence of non-trivial positive solutions to certain non-local equations defined on compact Riemannian manifolds. Specifically, we demonstrate that if a best Sobolev inequality exists, then non-trivial solutions to $( -\Delta )^m u = U^{\frac{N+\alpha}{p-\alpha}}$ (where $m$ is an integer) can be found under specific conditions.

Accurately estimating the paths of multiple objects is vital for applications like air traffic control and autonomous driving. While existing methods typically rely on forward simulation to model object motion, they often fail to account for the full state space, leading to inaccurate path predictions. To address this, we introduce a backward simulation approach that constrains object trajectories by modeling the probability of detection. By combining forward and backward simulations, we identify the most probable trajectories within the defined state space. Experiments conducted on two real-world datasets demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms current forward simulation approaches in terms of overall accuracy.

This paper presents a new method for evaluating multi-infeed grid-linked voltage-source converter (VSC) systems, based on modeling the VSCs as components of an admittance matrix. The approach involves deriving a model that represents a VSC using a two-port network, which is then integrated into the broader admittance matrix model of the entire system. This technique is applied to assess the stability of a multi-infeed VSC system by analyzing the eigenvalues of the system matrix derived from a linearized state-space model. The study further demonstrates the method's practicality through a case study of a multi-infeed HVDC system, where the results are compared against the conventional multi-machine power system stability model.

This study examines the intrinsic complexity of handwritten signatures and evaluates the repeatability of the unique writing styles observed. The research investigates the long-term stability of this intricacy and the consistency of the user's script to determine the maximum number of signatures that can be generated. Utilizing the fractal dimension as a metric for signature complexity, the analysis reveals that signatures possess a fractional dimension lower than 2, indicating they do not completely fill the two-dimensional plane. Statistical findings demonstrate that signature complexity remains relatively stable over time, with a calculated intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.81.

In this paper, we examine two distinct geometric frameworks for Hardy sums. The first framework is grounded in the theory of hyperplane arrangements, specifically utilizing the concept of a chamber complex. The second framework relies on the theory of posets, structured around a specialized poset named the "chamber poset." We demonstrate that the chambers within the chamber complex correspond exactly to the posets in the chamber poset, thereby establishing a direct equivalence between these two approaches.

This paper introduces a novel context management approach for C++ that utilizes a context stack to model a hierarchy of increasingly abstract levels. Unlike traditional mechanisms, this stack does not rely on nested function calls; instead, it allows distinct code blocks to access and inherit a common set of static values shared across a broader scope. We present a proposal for an extension to the C++ language that treats values defined outside function boundaries as strata, with an automatic mechanism to bind these values to specific code blocks. This feature facilitates the creation of modular and self-contained units capable of referencing contextual data external to their immediate scope.

This study introduces a novel 3D human pose recognition framework designed for monocular video sequences. The proposed architecture employs dilated convolutions to extract spatial features and temporal convolutions to capture dynamics, integrating both modules within a unified structure. To enhance performance, we developed an attention-based module that aggregates temporal cues across multiple scales. This module integrates information from diverse temporal scales, significantly boosting recognition accuracy. Experiments conducted on the dense pose dataset, which tracks human joints, demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches by a substantial margin.

The CZTI instrument aboard the Indian Astro Mission AstroSat is designed to observe X-ray and gamma-ray sources, but its field of view is restricted to approximately 10 degrees. To overcome this limitation, we propose utilizing occultation techniques with Earth, Moon, and the Sun to map the CZTI's response. This method involves analyzing the resulting occultation light curves to extract key spectral characteristics, including the mean flux, mean energy, and spectral index. By combining these measurements with a collimated beam, we can simulate the occultation light curves for celestial bodies of any desired size. Consequently, this approach enables the spectroscopic analysis of extended sources, such as the Milky Way, the Sun, and the Moon, effectively extending the CZTI's utility as an all-sky X-ray detector.

Blockchain technology is rapidly expanding across numerous sectors, yet its widespread adoption faces hurdles, particularly regarding the lack of a standardized framework for evaluating protocol efficiency. This study introduces a generalized method to assess the efficiency of various distributed ledger systems, encompassing blockchain protocols, to address this gap. By defining a specific set of parameters, the approach enables the comparison of protocols with differing structures and operational modes. Through a comprehensive analysis of 17 blockchain protocols, the study derives critical insights into their efficiency. The findings indicate that protocols utilizing block-based structures are generally more efficient than those based on trees, while those employing a round-robin consensus mechanism outperform others in efficiency.

We investigate the mass spectra of doubly heavy tetraquarks ($QQ\bar{q}\bar{q}$) within a chromomagnetic interaction model enhanced by a novel parameter. Our results indicate that the energy spectrum is highly sensitive to this parameter, which is derived from the interaction between heavy quarks and light quarks. By analyzing the mass spectrum of the $BB^*$ system, we determine the value of the chromomagnetic interaction parameter. Using this value, we calculate the mass spectrum for other doubly heavy tetraquarks ($QQ\bar{q}\bar{q}$) and compare our predictions with existing experimental data.

The Standard Model's parameter space is constrained by the vacuum stability condition, which dictates that the Higgs field must not roll down to a deeper minimum. This stability requirement is particularly crucial for the light Higgs boson, as its discovery at the LHC has established a lower bound on its mass that ensures the Higgs field remains trapped in the electroweak vacuum. We demonstrate that this vacuum stability constraint also yields a lower limit on the Higgs boson's decay rate into a pair of $Z$ bosons. This prediction arises because the Higgs field must not only be light but must also possess a sufficiently shallow potential well to avoid destabilization. By analyzing the interplay between the Higgs boson's mass and its coupling to $Z$ bosons, we find that the measured branching ratio into $ZZ$ is bounded from below, providing a novel test of the Standard Model. This result offers a direct probe of the Higgs potential's shape and provides an independent verification of the vacuum stability condition. This finding is significant because it

This paper establishes a $q$-logarithmic Sobolev inequality for the Carnot group, which is a specific type of stratified Lie group. Furthermore, it demonstrates a $p$-Talagamb inequality featuring a distance metric defined by the sub-Riemannian structure of Carnot spaces. Finally, it proves a $q$-version of the Reilly conjecture on these spaces, which are fundamental examples in sub-Riemannmann geometry.

This study investigates the problem of estimating $Y$ from $X$ by approximating the conditional distribution $P(Y|X)$ within a specific family of distributions $\mathcal{F}$, where $Y$ belongs to a discrete space $\mathcal{Y}$ and $\mathcal{F}$ is parameterized by $\theta \in \Theta$. The approach minimizes the Bregman divergence between the true conditional distribution $P(Y|X)$ and the model $P_\theta(Y|X)$, averaged over the distribution of $X$. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the optimal parameters $\hat{\theta}$ and derive a closed-form expression for them. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these findings extend to scenarios involving missing data, enabling the identification of a generative model for a Bayesian network's unknown components. Finally, we present an application of this framework to natural language processing.

This paper introduces a novel approach to view synthesis for real-world dynamic scenes using sparse, single-camera monocular inputs. Unlike existing techniques that depend on multiple cameras or extensive prior knowledge, our method employs a streamlined yet effective architecture to generate photorealistic results for arbitrary viewpoints. We achieve this by leveraging a combination of a 2D-3D correspondence network and a 3D-3D correspondence model, which jointly optimize the reconstruction of a 3D scene. To address the inherent ambiguities in monocular data, we incorporate a robust regularizer that enforces geometric and physical consistency. Our comprehensive experiments on various real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in both qualitative and quantitative metrics. Additionally, we have released the source code and datasets publicly to facilitate further research.

This study investigates a spectral statistic of two-dimensional quantum graphs that does not incorporate the semiclassical boundary condition. We demonstrate that this statistic consists of a sum of contributions derived from periodic orbits of all possible prime and composite forms. Crucially, these orbits include those that extend to infinity, provided they return to their points of origin. We establish the specific weights of these orbit-based terms through a direct comparison with the corresponding semiclassical statistic that includes the boundary.

This paper introduces a new method for determining the periods of periodic variable stars. The approach involves plotting the differences between consecutive light curve magnitudes against their corresponding ordinal numbers, followed by applying a low-pass filter to smooth the resulting data. The resulting light curve differences are then analyzed to identify peaks, with the distance between these peaks representing the variable star's period. This technique was tested on both real and synthetic datasets, yielding results that align well with those from established methods.

This paper addresses the challenge of finding the nearest NI framework to a given, generally non-NI, configuration within this domain. This paper presents the development of a self-supervised, end-to-end automatic speech recognition framework designed for unilingual applications. The system utilizes a Transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture, where the encoder processes audio inputs and the decoder generates textual outputs. We introduce a novel self-supervised training method capable of functioning without external transcription data. This approach involves creating a synthetic dataset by converting existing text into audio, enabling the model to learn directly from this generated content. We also conduct an evaluation on the impact of data augmentation techniques, specifically examining the efficacy of noise augmentation and speed perturbation. Additionally, we assess the performance of the model across various languages to determine its effectiveness in multilingual scenarios.

Code-switching refers to the practice of alternating between two or more languages within a single conversation. While numerous studies have examined code-switching in social media, few have addressed code-switching in conversational text. This study presents a deep learning model designed to classify emotions in code-switching, a task that was previously unexplored. The model was evaluated on the SemEval-2020 Task 9, which involves categorizing text into five emotion categories: joy, anger, sadness, disgust, and anticipation. The model achieved an F1 score of 0.51 on the test set.

This study examines a minimal three-loop radiative seesaw framework that simultaneously incorporates a mechanism for small-scale flavor mixing, an explanation for leptogenesis, and a dark energy sector. The model features a right-handed neutrino mass matrix driven by the vacuum expectation value of a scalar field, which is a dark energy candidate. This field's potential is constructed from the Froggatt-Nielsen mechanism, where the right-handed neutrinos possess specific charges. The resulting dark energy scale is approximately $10^{-3}$ eV, aligning with observational data. The mass matrix's structure is dictated by the Yukawa couplings of the right-handed neutrinos to the scalar field; these couplings are also responsible for generating the observed flavor mixing patterns. The study demonstrates that the Yukawa coupling hierarchy accounts for the mixing observed in the third generation of charged leptons. Furthermore, the model successfully reproduces the observed baryon asymmetry of the universe via thermal leptogenesis, with right-handed neutrino masses around $10^{14}$ GeV. The paper concludes by analyzing the model's parameter space, confirming its viability.

Neural networks have recently demonstrated significant success in predicting human reactions. This study introduces a novel item-based neural network designed to forecast individual responses to specific stimuli. The model employs a dual-architecture approach: first, an item network generates a representation for each stimulus, and second, a user network utilizes these representations to model interactions between users and stimuli for reaction prediction. We evaluated the system on two public datasets, achieving performance that surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we conducted ablation studies to assess the impact of various architectural choices and analyzed the learned item representations to examine the model's internal behavior.

This study introduces a robust collaborative design for an IRS-augmented cell-free network, accounting for both channel estimation errors and hardware imperfections. To address these challenges, we adopt a Bayesian framework to model the inherent uncertainties affecting both the IRS-to-user links and the power beams generated by each access point. Consequently, we formulate a min-max optimization problem aimed at enhancing the worst-case user rate by accounting for the worst-case estimation errors. To solve this, we develop a two-phase robust collaborative design: first, a robust IRS phase optimization that jointly refines the phase shifts and estimation error variances; second, a robust AP phase optimization that jointly adjusts the power allocation and error variances. To ensure computational tractability, we transform the min-max optimization into a standard form and employ a successive convex approximation algorithm to derive a suboptimal yet efficient solution. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that this proposed robust design outperforms existing benchmarks in terms of user rate performance.

This study investigates deep learning techniques for dynamically forecasting branch performance. We introduce a new dataset comprising 1,000 branch time series, each containing 1,000 weekly records of total revenue. We utilize a recurrent neural network (RNN) to model the temporal dependencies within this data. The performance of the RNN is benchmarked against a linear regression model and a gradient boosting machine (GBM). The findings indicate that the RNN outperforms both the linear regression model and the GBM in terms of forecasting accuracy.

This study introduces a novel active camera system utilizing deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) to prioritize target tracking. The system employs a mimicry-inspired strategy, where the camera's field of view (FOV) is positioned to match the location of the primary object outside it, ensuring the primary target remains outside the current frame. To achieve this, the method integrates two DCNNs: the External Network (ENet) tracks the main object, while the Internal Network (INet) assesses the likelihood of a primary target appearing within the current FOV. The INet is trained to identify the optimal viewing angle for the primary target, while the ENet is trained to locate the primary target. This article introduces a disordered Ising model in three dimensions, specifically the Potts-SOS model, which incorporates a third-state spin corresponding to a dislocation. We establish the existence of a Gibbs measure featuring a non-linear second-order disparity singularity. This finding is significant because it represents a new phenomenon not previously observed in this framework.

We introduce a novel phenomenon known as the "entangled" or "correlated" exchange of photon energy, occurring between two laser beams traveling in the same direction through an arbitrary medium. This interaction is mediated by a specific frequency shift in the spectral distribution of one beam, caused by the resonant absorption of photons from the co-propagating partner. This phenomenon is general, occurring in any medium regardless of its specific properties, and is distinguished by its adaptability to various spectral and spatial configurations.

This study examines the interaction between heavy quark mesons and those composed of light quarks, specifically focusing on the coupling constants between charmed and bottom mesons with their respective light vector mesons ($f_\rho$, $f_K$, $f_\omega$, and $f_J/\psi$). Utilizing QCD sum rules, we evaluate the coupling coefficients for the following processes: $D^{(*)} \to \rho^{(*)} V$, $D_s^{(*)} \to K^{(*)} V$, $B^{(*)} \to \rho^{(*)} V$, and $B_s^{(*)} \to K^{(*)} V$. Our findings indicate that the coupling coefficients for heavy mesons are highly sensitive to the chosen meson mass and decay constant. Furthermore, we observe that the coupling coefficients for $B^{(*)} \to \rho^{(*)} V$ and $B_s^{(*)} \to K^{(*)} V$ are substantially larger than those for $D^{(*)} \to \rho^{(*)} V$ and $D_s^{(*)} \to K^{(*)} V$. This suggests that the interaction between heavy quark mesons and those made of light quarks is stronger in bottom mesons compared to charmed mesons.

The global neutrino community is poised for a transformative era, characterized by an unprecedented array of upcoming experiments and observations. This paper offers a comprehensive overview of these future neutrino sources, highlighting their unique characteristics, anticipated sensitivities, and potential scientific contributions.

In causal analysis, researchers often rely on observational data to estimate causal effects within linear regression models. To address selection bias, these models incorporate covariates as adjustment factors. This study examines the optimal weighting strategy for such adjustments specifically in the linear framework. We demonstrate that using weights formulated as the inverse of adjusted covariate distributions—specifically, inversely weighted by adjusted covariate means—is suboptimal. Instead, we introduce a weighted least squares method utilizing a weighted regression of the adjustment factors themselves. This new approach offers two distinct advantages: it yields more precise causal effect estimates and produces more accurate predictions for adjusted covariate means compared to weight schemes based on the inverse of adjusted covariate means.

This paper introduces a novel Model-Free Wide-Area Model-Free Wide-Region Damping Control Framework (WDC) for enhancing the damping of electromagnetically interconnected oscillatory modes in power systems. The system leverages synchronized phasor data from widely dispersed points to capture comprehensive dynamic information. The control architecture comprises two primary components: a mode selection module utilizing a pre-trained neural network to identify electromagnetically coupled oscillatory modes, and a mode-based damping controller designed to suppress these modes. The selection module is trained offline using a dataset of mode selections and corresponding system states. The controller operates in real-time by determining the optimal control signal based on the identified mode, utilizing a pre-trained neural network that maps mode indices to optimal control inputs. The proposed WDC approach is validated on a modified IEEE 118-bus test system, demonstrating its effectiveness in damping electromagnetically coupled oscillatory modes.

We investigate the quantum dynamics of two atoms within a cavity, where their collective superradiance is balanced by a non-cooperative interaction that limits population. While the superradiant mechanism drives excitation toward a symmetric, long-lived subradiant state, the non-cooperative force prevents the system from reaching this state indefinitely. By analyzing the competition between these forces, we identify a specific interaction strength that allows for a unique steady state. In this regime, the subradiant lifetime of the two-atom system matches the timescale of the non-cooperative interaction, enabling precise control over the system's coherence duration.

This study examines the long-term behavior of a kink solution in a perturbed $\phi^6$ model featuring internal oscillations, subject to an odd perturbation. We demonstrate that when this perturbation is sufficiently small, both spatial kink positions and internal oscillation frequencies remain stable over time. Furthermore, we establish a quantitative link between the magnitude of the disturbance and the decay rate of the oscillation frequency.

The Japan Proton Accelerator Research Complex (J-PARC) is scheduled to commence beam operations in 2021, aiming to advance the understanding of the nuclear and hadron sciences. This article examines upcoming J-PARC initiatives focused on the study of color transparency, alongside an exploration of the scientific motivations behind these experiments.

Consistency training is a recently introduced paradigm designed to enhance the robustness of neural networks against input perturbations. While previous approaches predominantly focus on continuous perturbations, this paper introduces Consistency Training with Virtual Opponent Discrete Perturbation (CVOD), which extends consistency training to discrete perturbations. This method is particularly valuable for addressing tasks involving discrete inputs, such as natural language processing. We demonstrate that the CVOD framework is applicable to both supervised and unsupervised learning scenarios. Experimental results indicate that CVOD achieves state-of-the-art performance on two natural language processing benchmarks, surpassing both conventional training methods and existing consistency training techniques.

Endoscopy is a widely used, minimally invasive procedure for diagnosing colorectal polyps, which are frequently linked to colorectal cancer. While computer-aided detection (CAD) systems offer a promising solution to assist physicians, the inherent variability in endoscopic video quality and the lack of standardized annotation protocols have hindered the development of robust models. To address these challenges, this study introduces a multi-frame cooperative framework designed to enhance detection accuracy. The approach leverages a spatial-temporal feature transformation module that extracts and aligns salient information across multiple frames, thereby improving the overall performance of polyp detection. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Kvasir dataset.

Sampling within streams is a standard technique for estimating population parameters, yet most existing methods presume uniform distribution across the domain. This study addresses scenarios where data is non-uniformly distributed, introducing a new algorithm specifically designed for streaming contexts. This approach ensures that every individual possesses a predetermined, uneven sampling probability. The paper outlines a step-by-step implementation of the method and demonstrates its efficacy through various case studies.

The $rp$-process, which occurs in the most proton-rich nuclei, is critical for synthesizing elements in the $A \sim 60–90$ range during the explosive thermal evolution of massive stars. A key mechanism in this process is the bypass of reaction cycles that would otherwise lead to neutron-rich nuclei, effectively halting the flow at specific "pause points." While previous research identified a bypass at the $^{56}$Ni stopping point, the exact nature of this mechanism remained unclear. This study addresses that gap by measuring the $\beta$-delayed proton branching ratio for $^{57}$Zn, yielding a value of $P_{p} = 0.0010 \pm 0.0008$. This result confirms that $^{57}$Zn predominantly decays into $^{57}$Cr rather than proceeding via a bypass to $^{56}$Ni. Furthermore, the measured branching ratio aligns with the theoretical prediction of $P_{p} = 0.0009$ derived from a recent study of $^{57}$Zn's decay energy. These findings validate the proposed bypass mechanism, demonstrating that $^{57}$Zn decay effectively terminates at $^{57}$Cr, thereby preventing the formation of neutron-rich nuclei.

This paper investigates rational points defined over an algebraic closure within algebraic pencils on varieties. We establish a new theorem describing the distribution of these rational points on fibers of fibrations over bases. This theorem is applied to both uniform and non-uniform scenarios of the uniformed Manin-Mondford problem on abelian varieties and to a non-uniform variant of the problem concerning hyperelliptic curves.

This study presents an analysis of Very High Energy (VHE) gamma-ray emission from 16 selected pulsars located in the Northern Sky, utilizing 10 years of data from the VERITAS telescope array. The search strategy involves searching for both pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe) and pulsars themselves, with the latter being the primary focus. For the latter, we employ a novel search technique that incorporates the known pulsar positions and their proper motion into the analysis. For the former, we utilize a standard circular region of interest (ROI) centered on the associated PWNe. The analysis utilizes a likelihood-ratio test, comparing a hypothesis that includes the source signal against a null hypothesis assuming no source. The resulting 95% confidence upper limits on the flux are reported across a 0.1–30 TeV energy spectrum. No significant evidence for VHE emission was found in any of the studied pulsars or their associated PWNe.

This study examines reaction-diffusion equations featuring nonlocal boundary conditions on uneven domains. By analyzing the local model first, we derive conditions under which a unique solution exists within a specific time interval. Subsequently, we investigate how the solution's long-term asymptotic behavior is governed by the reaction term, utilizing a comparison principle to identify scenarios where the solution remains bounded over time.

Ultra-Compact Dwarfs (UCDs) are massive, dense stellar systems that are believed to be stripped cores of globular clusters or dwarf galaxies. This study utilizes an Explainable AI (XAI) approach to identify extragalactic UCDs within the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) database. We developed a Random Forest (RF) classifier to distinguish UCDs from other stellar populations, achieving a test set accuracy of 90.1%. To ensure the reliability of these classifications, we applied a Gradient Boosting Machine (GAM) to map the decision boundaries and confirm the physical plausibility of the model's results. Additionally, we introduced a new method to differentiate UCDs from Globular Cluster Groups (GCGs), a category previously lacking clear distinction in the literature. This approach yielded an 88.8% accuracy rate on the test set. The GAM analysis revealed that the primary differentiator between UCDs and GCGs is the slope of the luminosity-radius relationship, with UCDs exhibiting a steeper gradient.

Simulations are a powerful tool for investigating complex systems, offering a cost-effective and efficient approach to understanding system dynamics. Their application within recommendation systems has been explored in various contexts, including user modeling, churn prediction, and click-through rate analysis. This paper examines the current status of simulations in this field and identifies key obstacles, specifically the absence of standardized simulation protocols and limited access to proprietary data. We propose that advancing research in this area requires developing a unified methodology, fostering cross-disciplinary collaboration, and creating a standardized framework for evaluation.

This study investigates the hypothesis testing of truncated sample averages designed for extreme heavy-tailed distributions. The test statistic's asymptotic behavior is derived using the generalized method of moments, with the method's efficacy demonstrated through the application of the proposed approach to empirical data.

This study introduces a streamlined, high-performance approach for Motor Imagery (MI) classification within Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) systems, utilizing a hybrid model of Sinc filters and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The proposed method, termed Sinc-CNN, leverages the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to derive Sinc filter coefficients, which are subsequently integrated into the CNN framework. This architecture is designed to automatically identify key spectral features from raw EEG signals. The model was evaluated on the BCI Competition IV 2a dataset, which contains data from 9 subjects regarding the visualization of left, right, and common motor tasks. The results demonstrate that the Sinc-CNN model achieves an average classification accuracy of 80.5% across all subjects and tasks, surpassing other existing methods. Furthermore, the model exhibits robust generalization, maintaining consistent performance regardless of the subject or task involved.
We demonstrate that the recently proposed noncommutative version of $AdS_2$ possesses a precise correspondence with $AdS_2$ under the framework of the Gell-Mann Low theorem.

This study examines an ideal scenario for transplanting incompatible kidney pairs, where a single desensitization treatment can resolve the incompatibility for both donor-recipient pairs simultaneously. The analysis incorporates waiting lists for patients and available donor-recipient compatible pairs, alongside the specific duration of the treatment process. It determines optimal timing for initiating the procedure to maximize the number of transplants completed within a fixed period. The findings indicate that the ideal start time is not invariably the earliest possible date; rather, it depends on the volume of existing compatible pairs and the length of their matching queues.

This study introduces a hybrid Markov-LSTM model designed to enhance the predictive accuracy of both components. The Markov component utilizes the current system state to determine the probability of a specific action, while the LSTM network predicts the system state based solely on the chosen action. By integrating these two modules, the proposed framework achieves superior performance compared to standalone versions of either LSTM or Markov models. Furthermore, the modular design allows for easy adaptation to various domains, including but not limited to, recommendation systems, reinforcement learning, and natural language processing.

This paper investigates the boundedness and compactness properties of generalized integral operators acting on weighted Bergman spaces over bounded, strictly pseudoconvex domains in $\mathbb{C}^n$. The discussion includes an examination of generalized integral operators within standard weighted Bergman spaces on the unit polydisc and unit ball of $\mathbb{Q}^n$, where $n \geq 1$. Additionally, we explore the correspondence between generalized integral operators acting on these spaces and the associated Toeplitz operators.

At Qualtrics, we operate a vast array of machine learning models across numerous languages, including English, French, and German, alongside various other tongues. This paper introduces a cross-language multi-task learning framework designed to compress model weights into a compact, shared representation. This approach enables the deployment of a single, universal model capable of handling multiple language tasks. By applying this framework to our Qualtrics cross-language multi-job model, we reduced the model size by 85% while maintaining performance parity with our original separate models. Furthermore, we detail the operational challenges faced during implementation and their corresponding resolutions.

In the realm of data science, the phrase "garbage in, garbage out" serves as a fundamental reminder that the quality of a model's output is contingent upon the quality of its input data. This principle is especially critical in the field of medical image analysis, where data quality is paramount. This paper offers a critical examination of the challenges associated with medical image data, focusing on the complexities of data collection, the nuances of data labeling, and the issues surrounding class imbalance.

We demonstrate that decomposed Richelot mappings, which apply to hyperelliptic curves of even genus $g \geq 4$, are generally not surjective. Furthermore, we establish that the image of such a decomposition under Richelot mapping forms a Jacobian variety associated with a curve of lower genus. This result extends the findings of Howe regarding genus 4 curves, confirming that these constructed image varieties constitute ordinary Jacobians of specific hyperelliptic curves rather than being surjective across the entire Jacobian of a lower genus curve.

We present the discovery of three magnetic hot subdwarf B (sdB) stars, designated SDSS J002252.3+182850.3, SDSS J002222.3+182850.3, and SDSS J002222.3+182850.3, which exhibit magnetic field strengths of 1.3, 1.3, and 1.3 kG respectively. These stars are identified as the first magnetic sdB stars with measured rotational velocities exceeding 100 km/s. Our analysis of their spectra reveals that the magnetic field strength increases with stellar rotation, a trend consistent with the observed relationship between rotation and magnetic field strength in magnetic hot subdwarf A (sdBA) stars. Furthermore, we find that the magnetic field strength of these stars is positively correlated with their rotation speed, a pattern that mirrors the correlation between rotation and magnetic field strength in magnetic hot subdwarf A (sdBA) stars.
